study.title: Reimagining Construction Management Education in the Age of AI: Pathways to a 90-Credit Degree
study.abstract: Between 2024 and 2026 the institutional accreditors of the United States opened routes to bachelor’s degrees below 120 credits, and a federal rule of October 2026 tells them not to bar such degrees when outcomes are comparable; yet no construction program has taken one. This study asks how a construction management program could reach 90 credits while keeping what the profession needs, and what AI changes in that design. Framed as constraint-based curriculum design, it asks two questions of every design: is it feasible, meeting the credit and accreditation constraints at once, and is it adequate, preserving the learning outcomes and competencies the profession needs? Written rules sorted every required course of 81 accredited or applicant programs into course groups, and an integer program found, for each program, the smallest degree that satisfies its state, its institutional and programmatic accreditors and its own topics. Four findings stand out. First, the 17 learning outcomes of the American Council for Construction Education (ACCE) are not what keeps a program above 90: the construction courses that name them take a median 30 hours against ACCE’s floor of 50, and held to the outcomes alone every program fits, although the same floor is what keeps the internship in most designs. Second, geography outweighs design: moving the typical program across a state line adds 13 credits, twice what all its merges save, and the six states that ask 37 to 43 hours of general education, Texas and California among them, hold 33% of construction manager jobs while none of their programs reaches 90 at ACCE’s floors on its own. Third, a 90-credit degree need not be thinner: 68 programs teach course pairs that others already teach as one course, and 40 reach 90 keeping every topic once 12 major hours count as general education. Fourth, AI cannot pay for the cut, since the digital tool courses it could absorb hold a mean 4.6 credits, but it marks where merging is safe: its exposure peaks in the groups that carry estimating, scheduling and digital technology and is lowest in materials, structures and building systems. ACCE’s rule that business be taught apart keeps accounting and law taught twice in 30 and 26 programs. The median student would gain $91,047, a gain that pay 3.2% lower over a career would cancel, so the first students should be those who lose least. The study offers a map of course groups and an order of pathways: merge first, count major courses as general education second, and judge outcomes rather than hours third.
study.keywords: reduced-credit degree; curriculum design; course merging; general education; accreditation; construction management; artificial intelligence
rqs: RQ1. Where does the 90-credit construction degree stand in 2026, and what must a 90-credit construction degree satisfy?
RQ2. By which pathways, cutting to the accreditor’s floor, merging course groups and counting major courses as general education, could a program reach 90 credits, and what would each keep?
RQ3. How does AI change which course groups can be merged or compressed and which learning outcomes must be protected?
RQ4. What would a 90-credit degree give and take from students, institutions, employers and the profession, and what should programs, states and accreditors do first?
hypotheses: H1. Adequacy is not what makes most designs infeasible: the courses that preserve ACCE’s outcomes fit in a fraction of a 90-credit degree, and its hour floor, not its outcomes, decides feasibility.

H2. Feasibility under ACCE’s floors breaks at a general education count the rules predict: ACCE’s 62 professional hours plus the count, less the 3 hours of economics that count toward both, fit 90 only up to a count of 31, so the state a program sits in matters more than its design.

H3. Merging the course pairs the field already teaches as one course preserves every topic while freeing hours, so that with major courses counted as general education a substantial share of programs reach designs that are both feasible and adequate.
H4. AI-exposed work sits in course groups that carry few hours, so AI cannot make a design feasible on its own, but it marks the groups where adequacy can be kept in fewer hours.
theory: A 90-credit degree is a design problem in Simon’s sense: among the many curricula a program could offer, the task is to find one that meets every constraint adequately, since an optimum on all of them at once can rarely be had (Simon, 1996, chap. 5). This study frames the problem by two conditions that a design must meet together.

The first is curricular feasibility: whether any design fits 90 credits while meeting, at once, the general education count of the state and of the institutional accreditor, the programmatic accreditor’s hours and topics, and the institution’s own rules (Table 2). Feasibility is a property of the constraints together, not of any one of them: a degree can be infeasible although no single requirement asks for more than 90 credits. Curricular analytics has shown that the structure of a curriculum can be measured and compared across institutions (Heileman et al., 2018); feasibility adds the credit and accreditation constraints to that structure and asks whether the space of acceptable designs is empty.

The second is educational adequacy: whether a design keeps what the degree is for. Under constructive alignment, the intended outcomes are used to align teaching methods and assessment (Biggs, 1996), and backward design begins from the results a curriculum must produce and the evidence that shows them (Wiggins & McTighe, 2005). The study takes the corollary that an outcome a curriculum neither teaches nor assesses is not met, so a shorter degree must keep a course for each outcome it names, and a merged course must carry the outcomes of both courses it replaces. Engineering accreditation moved toward outcomes when ABET adopted outcome-based criteria (Lattuca et al., 2006), but outcomes do not name everything a degree protects: supervised field practice rests on hours more than on any outcome.

The two conditions pull against each other, and the useful designs meet both. A design can be feasible and inadequate, as when a cut to the accreditor’s floor reaches 90 by dropping topics or the internship, or adequate and infeasible, as when a program keeps every course and stays above 90. The integer program of Section 4 makes the first condition its constraints and the second its rules for what a design must keep, and the pathways it compares differ in how much adequacy they give up for feasibility. Four hypotheses follow.

ai_evidence.text: Endoscopists’ adenoma detection rate in colonoscopies without AI fell from 28.4% to 22.4% after routine exposure to AI (1,443 patients)
Outside the frontier of what AI does well, knowledge workers using it were correct about 19 percentage points less often; inside it they completed 12.2% more tasks
Knowledge workers with more confidence in AI reported less critical thinking (319 workers)
Automation bias affects experts as well as novices, and training does not remove it
Operators who only monitor automation lose the skill to take over when it fails

Three risks for learners: deskilling, the loss of previously acquired skills; mis-skilling, the reinforcement of incorrect behavior due to AI errors or bias; never-skilling, the failure to develop essential competencies
Students using ChatGPT improved essay scores without more knowledge gain or transfer
AI raised productivity by 15% on average and by 30% for less skilled and less experienced workers
Intelligent tutoring systems raise test performance by a median .66 standard deviations across 50 evaluations
A tutor designed to give one step at a time rather than the full solution doubled learning gains in less time in a randomized crossover trial (median 49 minutes against a 60-minute class)
Open access to GPT-4 raised practice grades by 48% but lowered grades on an exam taken without AI by 17%; a tutor that gave teacher-designed hints removed that loss
ChatGPT produced construction schedules that were coherent but contained wrong tasks
Model-based estimating still leaves the estimator substantial work
Junior employment fell about 9% at firms adopting generative AI, through fewer hires (working paper)
